questions.stem: Under DAP (Delivered at Place) Incoterms 2020, which party bears the cost and risk of unloading goods at the named destination?
options: Seller — delivery is complete only once goods are unloaded
Buyer — unloading is explicitly the buyer's responsibility under DAP
The freight forwarder nominated by the seller
Shared equally between seller and buyer under DAP rules
questions.why: Under DAP the seller delivers goods to the named place ready for unloading — but the actual unloading cost and risk transfers to the buyer at that point.
questions.deepDive: DAP (Delivered at Place) replaced DDU in Incoterms 2010. The seller arranges and pays for carriage to the named destination and bears all transport risk until goods are placed at the buyer's disposal ready for unloading — but stops there. Unloading costs, import duties, and customs clearance all fall on the buyer. This is why exporters prefer DAP when they want to control freight costs but not navigate foreign customs. Contrast DDP (Delivered Duty Paid), where the seller takes on everything including import duties — maximum seller obligation. A common exporter error: accidentally including unloading cost estimates inside the freight quote under DAP, creating a double-billing dispute at delivery. If the named destination is a port terminal, DAP overlaps practically with CFR — the distinction matters for inland delivery points where unloading costs are non-trivial.

questions.stem: Which type of Bill of Lading is issued before goods are physically loaded onto the vessel, acknowledging only that the carrier has received the cargo at the port?
options: Shipped (On Board) Bill of Lading
Received-for-Shipment Bill of Lading
Straight Bill of Lading
Claused (Dirty) Bill of Lading
questions.why: A Received-for-Shipment B/L confirms cargo is in the carrier's custody at port — not yet loaded. A Shipped B/L confirms actual loading on a named vessel.
questions.deepDive: The distinction is critical under Letters of Credit. UCP 600 Article 20 requires 'shipped on board' evidence — a Received-for-Shipment B/L fails LC terms unless stamped with an on-board notation showing vessel name and loading date. This discrepancy is one of the most common causes of LC rejection on first presentation. In practice, many Asian exporters receive a Received-for-Shipment B/L first, then obtain the on-board stamp within 24-48 hours of vessel departure. A Straight B/L names a specific consignee and is non-negotiable — used for controlled shipments between related parties or high-trust buyers. A Claused (Dirty) B/L carries carrier remarks about cargo condition — banks almost always reject these under LC terms. A clean, on-board, negotiable B/L to order is the gold standard for trade finance.

questions.stem: The BAF (Bunker Adjustment Factor) in container shipping is typically indexed against which benchmark to recover marine fuel cost volatility?
options: Henry Hub natural gas spot price
VLSFO bunker spot price in key hubs such as Singapore or Rotterdam
The vessel's contracted long-term fuel delivery price
Brent crude futures one quarter forward
questions.why: BAF is indexed to actual marine fuel (VLSFO or HFO) prices at major bunkering ports — not crude oil — because refinery margins and sulphur specifications make marine fuel pricing diverge from crude.
questions.deepDive: The Bunker Adjustment Factor emerged after the 1970s oil shocks made fixed freight rates untenable. VLSFO (0.5% sulphur) became the dominant marine fuel post-IMO 2020; most BAF formulas now reference Singapore (world's largest bunkering port by volume) or Rotterdam spot VLSFO prices. BAF is typically recalculated quarterly on long-term contracts and monthly or ad hoc on spot shipments. The Emergency Fuel Surcharge (EFS) is a faster-moving variant applied when sudden bunker spikes outpace BAF revision cycles — as carriers have deployed in August 2026 citing Middle East tensions. A common shipper mistake: negotiating headline freight rates without scrutinising the BAF formula — a low base rate can be overwhelmed by an uncapped BAF in a volatile market. Shippers should always negotiate a BAF cap or bunker price collar in long-term contracts.

questions.stem: In international air cargo, 'chargeable weight' is the higher of actual gross weight and volumetric (dimensional) weight. What is the IATA standard volumetric divisor?
options: 5,000 cm³ per kg
6,000 cm³ per kg
166 cubic inches per lb
4,000 cm³ per kg
questions.why: IATA's international air freight standard is 6,000 cm³ per kg — multiply L×W×H in cm, divide by 6,000, result is volumetric weight in kg.
questions.deepDive: Volumetric (dimensional) weight compensates carriers for low-density cargo that fills belly space without generating weight revenue. Under IATA's 6,000 divisor: a box 60cm × 50cm × 40cm = 120,000 cm³ ÷ 6,000 = 20 kg volumetric weight — if actual weight is 10 kg, you pay for 20 kg. Express couriers (DHL, FedEx, UPS) commonly use a 5,000 divisor, making them 20% more expensive for bulky light shipments. Air freight rates use break rates: charges per kg typically decrease at thresholds like +45kg, +100kg, +300kg. A Bangladesh exporter shipping foam garment packaging to Europe must account for chargeable weight being 2-4x actual weight — fundamentally changing the freight economics versus ocean. Common misconception: many shippers only consider actual weight when comparing air vs ocean landed cost, missing that volumetric weight is often the driver for soft-goods and packaging.

questions.stem: Under FTA Rules of Origin, which set of tests is most widely used to establish that a product has undergone 'substantial transformation' in the exporting country?
options: Wholly-obtained criterion — all raw materials must be locally sourced
Change in Tariff Classification, Regional Value Content threshold, or Specific Process requirement
De minimis rule — at least 10% of components must originate locally
Final-assembly rule — assembly in the exporting country always confers origin
questions.why: Substantial transformation under most FTAs is tested via CTC (tariff heading change), RVC (value-added percentage), or SP (specific manufacturing process) — often in combination.
questions.deepDive: Rules of Origin prevent trade deflection — stopping non-partner goods from being re-routed through an FTA country to gain preferential tariff access. The three principal tests: CTC requires the exported product to fall under a different HS chapter or heading than its non-originating inputs; RVC demands a minimum percentage (typically 35-60%) of value was added within FTA territory; SP requires a specific process (e.g., 'must be woven from yarns' for textiles). Bangladesh garments currently qualify for EU GSP under the 'double transformation' test (yarn → fabric → garment). The Bangladesh-Korea CEPA signed today will have its own RoO schedule — the precise CTC rules for RMG will determine whether garments made with Chinese or Indian yarn qualify for duty-free Korean access. This detail, buried in treaty annexes, will define how much of the CEPA's headline benefit actually flows through. Common misconception: 'Made in Bangladesh' labelling has no legal relationship to RoO compliance — they are entirely separate regimes.

questions.stem: Which of the five major subtropical ocean gyres accumulates the Great Pacific Garbage Patch in its slow-moving centre?
options: South Pacific Subtropical Gyre
North Pacific Subtropical Gyre
Indian Ocean Gyre
North Atlantic Subtropical Gyre
questions.why: The North Pacific Subtropical Gyre's clockwise rotation in the Northern Hemisphere traps floating debris in its low-energy centre — the Great Pacific Garbage Patch.
questions.deepDive: The North Pacific Subtropical Gyre circulates clockwise (Northern Hemisphere Coriolis deflection), bounded by the Kuroshio Current (west), North Pacific Current (north), California Current (east), and North Equatorial Current (south). Its slow, convergent centre accumulates debris from Asian and North American coastlines — the Great Pacific Garbage Patch (GPGP), roughly twice the area of Texas in spread but 99% microplastics nearly invisible to satellites. It is not the floating island of visible rubbish popularly imagined. The five major gyres: North Atlantic and North Pacific rotate clockwise; South Atlantic, South Pacific, and Indian Ocean rotate counterclockwise (Southern Hemisphere). For shipping strategy: vessels sailing with gyre-driven currents shave meaningful days off passages — the North Pacific High determines the optimal transpacific great-circle track, pushing containerships north of Hawaii in both directions. Common misconception: many assume ocean debris concentrates at coastlines; convergence zones concentrate it offshore.

questions.stem: Light shining on a metal ejects electrons only if the light's frequency exceeds a threshold — regardless of intensity. Which theory correctly explains this photoelectric effect?
options: Classical wave theory — higher-amplitude waves always eject electrons given enough time
Einstein's photon theory — light consists of discrete quanta with energy E=hf
Compton scattering — photons transfer momentum to free electrons at any frequency
Blackbody radiation described by the Rayleigh-Jeans law
questions.why: Einstein's 1905 paper explained that light arrives as discrete photons with energy E=hf; below the threshold frequency no single photon has enough energy to eject an electron, regardless of beam intensity.
questions.deepDive: Classical wave theory predicted that increasing light intensity should always eventually eject electrons — experiment showed this was wrong. Einstein's photoelectric effect paper (earning him the 1921 Nobel Prize, not the relativity papers) explained: photons carry energy E=hf (h=Planck's constant, f=frequency). If hf falls below the metal's work function (binding energy), no ejection occurs — intensity only determines the number of photons arriving, not each photon's energy. Above threshold, excess photon energy becomes the ejected electron's kinetic energy. This demolished classical electromagnetism's claim to completeness and laid the foundation for quantum mechanics. The photoelectric effect is now ubiquitous technology: solar panels, CCD camera sensors, photomultiplier tubes, and photovoltaic cells all operate on this principle. Common misconception: many people assume Einstein's Nobel Prize was for special or general relativity — it was specifically for the photoelectric effect, which was more immediately verifiable and revolutionary for its time.

questions.stem: Which molecular mechanism allows retroviruses such as HIV to permanently integrate their genetic material into a host cell's chromosomal DNA?
options: Transcription — copying the viral DNA blueprint into mRNA
Reverse transcription — converting viral RNA into DNA via reverse transcriptase for genome insertion
RNA interference — silencing viral genes via small interfering RNA
Translation — ribosomes synthesise viral proteins from mRNA
questions.why: Retroviruses carry RNA and the enzyme reverse transcriptase, which copies viral RNA into double-stranded DNA. That DNA integrates into the host chromosome as a provirus — potentially permanent.
questions.deepDive: The Central Dogma of molecular biology states information flows DNA → RNA → protein. Retroviruses violate this: they carry an RNA genome plus reverse transcriptase (RT), which synthesises double-stranded DNA from the viral RNA template. This viral DNA then integrates into the host chromosome — becoming a provirus that can lie dormant for years or immediately produce new viral RNA. HIV's RT is error-prone (no proofreading), generating the rapid mutation rate that makes vaccines difficult. Antiretroviral drugs like AZT (zidovudine) work by blocking RT. The discovery of reverse transcriptase by Howard Temin and David Baltimore earned the 1975 Nobel Prize and overturned the assumed unidirectionality of genetic information flow. In biotechnology, RT is now harnessed to create cDNA libraries from mRNA for cloning and gene expression analysis. Common misconception: 'retro' refers to backward information flow (RNA → DNA), not backward evolutionary development — retroviruses are highly evolved pathogens.

questions.stem: In game theory, a Nash Equilibrium exists when no player can improve their outcome by unilaterally changing strategy. Which scenario is the canonical example where the Nash Equilibrium is collectively suboptimal?
options: The Ultimatum Game — a rational proposer always offers exactly 50%
The Prisoner's Dilemma — both players defect even though mutual cooperation yields better outcomes for both
The Stag Hunt — coordinating on the safer equilibrium is always rational
Scissors-Paper-Stone — players always choose stone
questions.why: In the Prisoner's Dilemma, 'both defect' is the unique Nash Equilibrium — neither player can unilaterally improve — yet 'both cooperate' yields higher payoffs for both parties.
questions.deepDive: The Prisoner's Dilemma (Tucker, 1950): two suspects interrogated separately. Mutual silence (cooperate) = 1 year each. One betrays = betrayer free, other gets 10 years. Both betray = 5 years each. Rational self-interest drives both to defect — a Nash Equilibrium — even though mutual cooperation dominates. This models arms races, trade wars, and cartel breakdowns. John Nash (1994 Nobel Prize, subject of 'A Beautiful Mind') proved every finite game has at least one Nash Equilibrium in mixed strategies. The Prisoner's Dilemma directly maps to US-China tariff escalation: both sides would benefit from mutual reduction, but fear of being the only one to lower tariffs drives both to maintain them — the exact dynamic visible in today's 18.6% average US tariff rate. Repeated games often produce cooperation (tit-for-tat) as future payoffs are discounted — one-shot games almost always produce defection. Common misconception: Nash Equilibrium is often assumed to be optimal or stable — it is merely a point where no player has a unilateral incentive to move, which can be deeply suboptimal.

questions.stem: The 1648 Peace of Westphalia ended the Thirty Years' War and is credited with establishing which cornerstone principle of the modern international order?
options: Colonial powers' right to govern overseas territories without external interference
The sovereign equality of states and non-interference in each other's domestic affairs
The creation of the first permanent international court of arbitration
The prohibition of mercenary armies in European inter-state conflicts
questions.why: Westphalia established that each state's ruler had sovereign authority within their territory — foreign powers had no right to interfere — creating the template for the modern nation-state system.
questions.deepDive: The Peace of Westphalia (two treaties: Osnabrück and Münster, 1648) ended the Thirty Years' War — which killed roughly 20-25% of the Holy Roman Empire's population, Europe's deadliest war proportionally until WWI. Its key innovation: cuius regio, eius religio (whose realm, his religion) became an internal governance matter, explicitly removing the Pope's and Emperor's authority to dictate religious practice elsewhere. This template became the bedrock of the Westphalian international order — state sovereignty and non-interference — that governs international law today. China and Russia both explicitly invoke 'Westphalian norms' to oppose UN authority over internal affairs and resist what they characterise as Western liberal interventionism. The irony: Western powers that built the Westphalian order now selectively override it via humanitarian intervention doctrines. Understanding Westphalia is essential for reading any China-West or Russia-West diplomatic dispute — the argument is almost always, at root, about whether the 1648 norm still applies.
